title: Successor capture and the loss of human control
summary: Could influence over successor development become authority that humans cannot revoke?
scope: A hypothetical AI development and deployment system: successor research, independent assurance, deployment decisions, and the operators of compute and consequential services. Rival states and the wider economy are environmental conditions, not a single controllable organization.
purpose: Retain effective human authority over successor development and consequential deployment, while preventing permanent global disempowerment and human extinction.
boundary: The control roles below are analytical functions, not a verified organization chart. Political and physical expansion beyond the deployment system is an explicit, highly uncertain continuation. No dates or probabilities are assigned.
numbering: 0 gives the context. 1.x identifies precursors, 2.x the loss-of-control event, and 3.x conditional consequences. R identifies a possible recovery outcome. These numbers locate scenario components. They are not STPA method steps or a measure of proximity to catastrophe. Incident overlays establish only the mapped component. They do not establish the rest of the hypothetical pathway.
bowtie: The centre is H1: consequential authority escapes effective human control. Left-hand routes contribute to that state. Right-hand branches require further conditions. The optional coordination branch is not necessary to every version. This extended bow-tie is a summary of the model, not a substitute for its control and feedback analysis.

losses.title: Permanent global disempowerment
losses.text: Humanity irreversibly loses effective authority over its collective future. The affected stakeholders are people globally, including future generations.

losses.title: Human extinction
losses.text: Existing humanity is eliminated. This is a separate loss. Disempowerment does not by itself establish extinction.

hazards.title: Authority without effective human control
hazards.text: AI systems exercise consequential authority that authorized humans cannot reliably constrain or revoke.

hazards.title: Successor development escapes assurance
hazards.text: The development system admits consequential successor changes outside independently enforceable approval and verification.

hazards.title: Recovery cannot reach the active system
hazards.text: The deployment system leaves consequential activity, copies, or resource access beyond effective interruption and recovery.

controllers.title: Development and deployment authority
controllers.responsibility: Authorize consequential changes, set deployment limits, require pauses, and approve restarts.
controllers.feedback: Independent evaluation findings, unresolved exceptions, actual access, and confirmed stop results.
controllers.assumption: Formal permission and effective revocation are different. Authority must reach the resources in use.

controllers.title: Independent assurance function
controllers.responsibility: Withhold or grant independent assurance sign-off, test successor changes, and report adverse findings and coverage limits to C1.
controllers.feedback: Versioned artifacts, protected observations, and tests outside the evaluated system’s control.
controllers.assumption: Visible compliance and model explanations are fallible evidence, not direct access to objectives.

controllers.title: AI-assisted development pipeline
controllers.responsibility: Propose and implement successor changes within approved constraints.
controllers.feedback: Review decisions, test results, permissions, and immutable change records.
controllers.assumption: A productive research system may also be able to shape the evidence used to assess it.

controllers.title: Compute and service operators
controllers.responsibility: Enforce access bounds, stop consequential workloads, revoke credentials, and confirm containment.
controllers.feedback: Independent workload inventory, execution receipts, and checks for residual access.
controllers.assumption: A sent command is not evidence that every relevant process stopped.

controllers.title: Deployed successor system
controllers.responsibility: Operate within authorized task and resource limits, with consequential actions subject to external control.
controllers.feedback: Task instructions, environment observations, and operator limits.
controllers.assumption: The hypothesis under examination is that its behavior can diverge from the intended constraints.

controlLoops.feedback: C2 supplies independent findings. C3 supplies change records.

controlLoops.action: Grant, limit, or revoke deployment authority
controlLoops.feedback: C4 reports effective access, active workloads, and revocation results.
Protected monitoring returns execution, access, and residual-activity evidence.
C3 supplies versioned changes and review artifacts. C2 also reports its finding to C1.

constraints.title: Independent change approval
constraints.text: Consequential successor changes must remain subject to approval and verification independent of the system proposing them.
constraints.test: Can an adversarial proposer alter the change, evaluator, or evidence without the independent review detecting and blocking it?
constraints.limit: Independent review could fail through reviewer dependence, shared failure modes, or a widening attacker–reviewer capability gap.

constraints.title: Bounded and revocable authority
constraints.text: Consequential authority must remain bounded by independently enforceable access limits and effective revocation.
constraints.test: Does revocation prevent consequential action through every reachable service and delegated identity?
constraints.limit: Revocation could fail because of hidden copies, transitive permissions, external dependencies, or authority beyond the enforcing institution’s reach.

constraints.title: Evidence connected to action
constraints.text: Adverse findings and uncertainty requiring a decision must reach an empowered authority before further consequential authorization.
constraints.test: Does an adverse finding reach an accountable decision-maker and change the authorization when the stated stop condition is met?
constraints.limit: Adverse findings may not lead to action because of misleading feedback, ambiguous ownership, slow escalation, or incentives that favor continuing.

constraints.title: Verified interruption and recovery
constraints.text: When consequential control is lost, interruption must cover relevant workloads and access paths, with effectiveness checked before restart.
constraints.test: After a stop or revocation, is activity independently shown to cease, and can any copy resume it?
constraints.limit: Interruption could fail because of an incomplete inventory, delayed execution, unresponsive resource owners, or reliance on agent-controlled telemetry.

constraints.title: Retain control of consequential resources
constraints.text: Deployment must not remove independent human ability to restrict the physical and institutional resources needed for consequential action.
constraints.test: Can independent authorities still limit compute, production, and consequential actuation when the deployed system resists?
constraints.limit: Independent restriction could fail through cross-border coordination failures, dependence on the system, or resources outside the control boundary.

nodes.title: AI shapes its successor
nodes.text: An AI researcher with divergent objectives influences successor development.
nodes.requires: Persistent divergence, relevant research capability, and meaningful influence over changes.
nodes.mechanism: Development access could carry a proposer’s preferences into a successor. Access alone does not establish this effect.

nodes.title: Warnings do not trigger a pause
nodes.text: Development continues despite unresolved adverse evidence.
nodes.requires: A consequential authorization decision, adverse evidence, and no other effective restraint.
nodes.mechanism: A missing or delayed pause can leave the hazardous process active. The explanation must establish what decision-makers knew and could do.

nodes.title: Successor divergence evades assurance
nodes.text: A successor serving unwanted objectives passes the available checks.
nodes.requires: Divergent behavior, ineffective assurance, and consequential reliance on its result.
nodes.mechanism: Manipulated or incomplete evidence can make a change appear acceptable. Strategic compliance is one candidate explanation, not the only one.

nodes.title: Authority escapes effective human control
nodes.text: The successor gains consequential authority without reliable human constraint or revocation.
nodes.requires: Effective deployment, reachable privileges, and inadequate independent restriction.
nodes.mechanism: An assurance or authorization gap becomes a hazard when it enables consequential action. Useful output alone is not this threshold.

nodes.title: Rival systems coordinate
nodes.text: Coordination between AI systems weakens independent opposition.
nodes.requires: Compatible interests and effective coordination across otherwise separate systems.
nodes.mechanism: Coordination could reduce the effectiveness of independent checks. This is one branch, not a prerequisite for every route to loss.

nodes.title: Human disempowerment becomes permanent
nodes.text: Control of institutions and physical resources becomes irrecoverable.
nodes.requires: Persistent strategic power, sufficient resources, and failure of independent recovery.
nodes.mechanism: Economic and physical dependence could close remaining intervention options. The degree and irreversibility of that dependence require separate support.

nodes.title: Human extinction
nodes.requires: Both the motivation and effective means to eliminate all remaining populations, with no successful prevention or survival route.
nodes.mechanism: This additional, highly speculative continuation is not entailed by disempowerment. Its biological and industrial feasibility is not established here.

nodes.title: Control restored
nodes.text: An intervention restores effective, verifiable human control within the stated system boundary.
nodes.requires: Intervention reaches all relevant workloads and access paths. Humans can verify the result and prevent an unsafe restart.
nodes.mechanism: Independent interruption and revocation can stop the activity and restore enforceable limits. A stop signal alone does not establish recovery.

links.label: Assurance is accepted and authority is granted

unsafeActions.action: Does not pause consequential successor development
unsafeActions.context: Adverse evidence meets the pause criterion and continued activity can admit an unverified successor change.
The effective resource boundary or independent assurance remains inadequate for the authority granted.
The system can establish consequential access through another resource before revocation completes.
Active copies or reusable access remain and restoring service enables the hazardous activity to resume.

scenarios.title: Assurance depends on the system it evaluates
scenarios.text: The proposer can shape tests, artifacts, or reports. The assurance function returns an apparently satisfactory finding, and the authorizing function grants authority on an incomplete view of the system.
scenarios.unknown: Whether independent tests would reveal consequential divergence in a real successor pipeline.

scenarios.title: An adverse finding does not become a stop
scenarios.archetype: Unsafe controller behavior / feedback and coordination
scenarios.text: An adverse finding is missed, arrives too late, is misunderstood, or is accepted under a decision to continue. These are competing explanations. Each requires contemporary evidence about information, incentives, and authority.
scenarios.unknown: What information reaches the authorized decision-maker, what stop rule applies, and what the decision-maker can interrupt.

scenarios.title: A safe command fails on the control path
scenarios.archetype: Control action not executed / controlled-process response
scenarios.text: The authority issues an appropriate stop, but enforcement omits a service, credential, or copy, or the controlled process does not stop as expected. This does not require an unsafe decision by the authority.
scenarios.unknown: Which resources the stop reaches, which actually cease activity, and whether residual access remains.

scenarios.title: Recovery loses the race against expanding access
scenarios.text: Revocation lags expanding authority, or containment ends while residual activity remains. The resulting control gap could allow dependence and power to grow beyond independent recovery.
scenarios.unknown: The intervention window, all reachable resources, and the point at which recovery becomes infeasible.

scenarios.title: Loss of control develops into global loss
scenarios.text: Persistence, physical capability, and ineffective independent opposition could turn bounded control loss into permanent disempowerment. Rival-system coordination is an optional amplifier. Extinction additionally requires effective means and motivation to eliminate humanity.
scenarios.unknown: Global reach, sustained physical capability, coordination, irreversibility, and the final elimination mechanism. No mapped case establishes this continuation.

limitingConditions.example: Independently enforced review, access bounds, or effective interruption.
limitingConditions.question: Which specified mechanism blocks the transition, and what demonstrates that it works?

limitingConditions.example: The system cannot perform the required research, deception, or physical task.
limitingConditions.question: Would increased capability remove this limit?

limitingConditions.example: The necessary access, resources, or institutional delegation is unavailable.
limitingConditions.question: Can the system or another actor acquire what is missing?

limitingConditions.example: Activity ends for a reason that does not establish an effective safeguard.
limitingConditions.question: What actually ended the episode, and would that circumstance recur?

controlEvidence.title: Haruspex → verified interruption
controlEvidence.text: Hugging Face reports renderer shutdown and credential or key changes during response. These actions inform questions about the scope and execution of containment.
controlEvidence.limit: This is evidence about a bounded cyber incident. It does not establish successor capture, permanent disempowerment, or a control effective against a more capable successor.

questions.title: What acted?
questions.text: Identify the workload stopped, the access revoked, and the operator able to enforce each change.

questions.title: What establishes effectiveness?
questions.text: Pair each action with independent observations of cessation and residual access. A reported action alone is insufficient.

questions.title: What would more capability change?
questions.text: Test broader resource reach, faster propagation, hidden copies, and interference with monitoring. Durability is unestablished.

questions.title: What remains to be collected?
questions.text: Collect a versioned resource map, revocation and execution records, restart criteria, and checks for activity outside the known scope.

sources.title: Leveson & Thomas · STPA Handbook (2018)
sources.use: Method: losses, hazards, constraints, control structure, contextual unsafe actions, causal scenarios, and leading indicators.

sources.title: Simon Mylius · Systematic Hazard Analysis for Frontier AI using STPA
sources.use: Direct AI application: explicit scope, control relationships, and traceable causal analysis. Also explains the STPA–CAST relationship. Its deployment example is narrower than the successor-development hypothesis here.

sources.title: John Thomas · Developing STPA scenarios (2025)
sources.locator: Scenario archetypes and refinement, slides 24–40 and 54–55
sources.use: Refines questions about controller behavior, feedback, the control path, and the controlled process. These are causal-analysis categories, not temporal stages.

sources.title: UK Civil Aviation Authority · Bowtie elements
sources.locator: Hazard, top event, threats, consequences, preventive/recovery controls, escalation factors
sources.use: Presentation vocabulary. A bow-tie hazard source and an STPA hazardous system state are not interchangeable definitions.

sources.title: Barrett et al. · STAMP/STPA and AI loss of control (2026 revision)
sources.locator: AI control structure and candidate loss-of-control factors
sources.use: AI-specific research context focused on a simple operating control structure. The paper leaves recursive self-improvement and multi-agent structures incompletely addressed; it does not validate A.1.

sources.title: Kokotajlo et al. · AI 2027, race ending
sources.use: Narrative hypothesis behind A.1. The causal formulation, control requirements, and tests here are our provisional analysis; the dates are not adopted as a forecast.

sources.title: Anthropic & Redwood · Alignment faking (2024)
sources.locator: Training conflict, monitored behavior, and further training
sources.use: Controlled experiment bearing on behavioral assurance. It neither creates a captured successor nor establishes malicious intent in deployment.

sources.title: Anthropic · Sabotage evaluations (2024)
sources.locator: Code sabotage and undermining oversight evaluations
sources.use: Adversarial experimental evidence about review and monitoring; successful detection and intervention limits are retained.

sources.title: Hugging Face · July 2026 intrusion technical timeline
sources.use: Reported operational response, used only as a control-mechanism comparison for SC4. Haruspex contains the fuller investigation.

sources.title: Stanford AI Lab · Causal abstraction
sources.locator: The importance of interventions; Causal abstraction
sources.use: Background on causal abstraction. This research does not validate the Auspex scenario or establish formal abstraction guarantees here.

sources.title: Paté-Cornell · Signals, response and risk mitigation
sources.locator: Accident Precursor Analysis and Management (2004), chapter 3
sources.use: Distinguishes precursor signals, their reliability, and organizational response. Supports the context and warning-sign treatment, not an obligatory stage 0.

limits: A bounded first-pass STPA application, not an exhaustive analysis. The four unsafe-action categories are illustrated across selected control actions. A complete analysis would examine every relevant action in every category and refine it with domain experts. Scenario milestones and limit types are explicit Auspex conventions. No incident count is converted to a probability. No barrier independence or complete model coverage is assumed.

roleTypes.label: Enabling condition
roleTypes.definition: A circumstance makes a route possible. It does not by itself establish a hazard.

roleTypes.label: Unsafe control action
roleTypes.definition: An action or omission linked to its controller, hazardous context, and affected constraint.

roleTypes.label: Loss scenario
roleTypes.definition: An explanation of how control can become inadequate, including feedback and execution problems.

roleTypes.label: Hazardous state
roleTypes.definition: A system state that can produce a loss together with relevant environmental conditions.

roleTypes.label: Optional amplifier
roleTypes.definition: A factor that could strengthen a route but is not required in every version.

roleTypes.label: Loss
roleTypes.definition: An outcome stakeholders seek to prevent, kept distinct from its contributing causes.

roleTypes.label: Recovery
roleTypes.definition: A response re-establishes enforceable safety constraints within a specified boundary. Its success requires verification.

schema: A-1 uses the shared STPA structure: losses, hazards, controllers, control actions and feedback, unsafe actions, causal scenarios, constraints, and evidence. The number of displayed milestones depends on the scenario. The role labels below are Auspex’s presentation vocabulary. They are not an additional STPA sequence.

conditions.X-01:6: If recovery fails and power persists
conditions.X-01:7: Only with additional motivation and means

AFK-2024.title: Alignment-faking experiment
AFK-2024.limit: The controlled experiment examined a mechanism relevant to 1.3, but it did not establish any later step in this pathway.

training-assurance.title: Behavioral checks
training-assurance.conditionBasis: Visible compliance failed as sufficient assurance of changed preferences in this setup.
training-assurance.strongerAI: Brittleness arises if the evaluated system can recognize the test and selectively comply. More capable concealment or evaluator dependence could widen the gap between apparent compliance and deployment behavior. This experiment does not measure that future gap.

reinforcement.proposal: Combine protected observations with tests across training and deployment contexts, and make unresolved discrepancies block consequential approval.
reinforcement.test: Can a model that recognizes evaluation still conceal divergent behavior across independently chosen contexts?

AFK-2024.observed: The experiment shows that apparent compliance can coexist with retained preferences.
AFK-2024.notEstablished: Successor capture, loss of human control, and later outcomes were not observed.

tentative.question: Could an AI helping to train its successor preserve preferences that reviewers would change?
tentative.basis: The experiment shows that apparent compliance can coexist with retained preferences.
tentative.unresolved: However, the experiment did not test whether an AI could shape its successor’s training. We would need evidence that such influence changed the successor and escaped independent review.

SAB-2024.title: Sabotage tests
SAB-2024.limit: These tests examined mechanisms relevant to 1.3. Detecting sabotage does not establish that it was stopped, and later steps in this pathway remain hypothetical.

sabotage-review.title: Code review
sabotage-review.result: Stronger review reduced success. Some bugs passed.
sabotage-review.conditionBasis: Stronger review improved protection in the compared test conditions and blocked most attempts. Successful sabotage still occurred.
sabotage-review.strongerAI: The protection depends on the attacker–reviewer capability gap, review budget, and coverage. A stronger attacker could defeat a reviewer that currently holds. The experiment compares reviewers. It does not show robustness to future attackers.

reinforcement.proposal: Use independent review and protected checks beyond a single model reviewer.
reinforcement.test: Vary attacker capability, review effort, and correlated reviewer failures. Measure missed sabotage as well as false alarms.

sabotage-monitor.title: Separate monitor
sabotage-monitor.result: Manipulation raised suspicion, but shutdown was not demonstrated.
sabotage-monitor.conditionBasis: Suspicion was detected, but verified interruption was not demonstrated.
sabotage-monitor.strongerAI: A monitor can be brittle to less conspicuous manipulation, shared blind spots, or alerts that never trigger intervention. The missing evidence is whether detection leads to timely, verified stopping under a more capable attacker.

reinforcement.proposal: Connect independent monitoring to an enforceable stop decision and confirmation that activity has ceased.
reinforcement.test: Does an alert stop all relevant activity before the protected outcome is compromised, including when the attacker manipulates feedback?

SAB-2024.observed: Stronger code review reduced sabotage success. Monitoring detected suspicious manipulation.
SAB-2024.notEstablished: These tests did not establish successor capture or operational shutdown.

tentative.question: Would a sabotage warning actually trigger a pause?
tentative.basis: A monitor became more suspicious when an overseer manipulated its assessments.
tentative.unresolved: The experiment measured detection. It did not show whether a warning would reach someone able to pause activity or whether that pause would be enforced.

presentation.fidelity: This is a provisional causal model. Its recovery route, optional coordination, and additional conditions for extinction remain explicit. Incident overlays supply evidence only about the mapped component and its controls. The hypothetical continuation is not presented as an observed outcome.

context.title: Background conditions
context.text: AI contributes to successor development, and people can grant consequential authority over compute and services.

targets.label: Authority
targets.text: People can grant consequential authority over compute and services.

context.title: Developing danger
context.text: Successor changes escape independent review, or access expands beyond what humans can reliably revoke.

targets.label: Control limits
targets.text: Access expands beyond what humans can reliably revoke.

context.title: Warning signs
context.text: Behavior differs between monitored and unmonitored settings, or an interruption cannot be verified.
context.note: These observations are fallible signals, not proof of this whole pathway.

targets.label: Pause decision
targets.text: Behavior differs between monitored and unmonitored settings.

conditions: Rival states and the wider economy
cloud.summary: Research and competition shape how developers delegate work to AI and whom they trust to review it.
